I know this because I was eleven the first time I went in, on a dare, on a Tuesday in September when the light goes gold and forgiving. My friends waited on the sidewalk with their bikes. No echo. My voice went out of me and simply kept going, the way a stone dropped into a very deep well goes on falling long after you've stopped expecting the splash.

Dozens of them, hundreds, layered down like rings in a tree, all of them still happening, all of them at once, all of them quiet as breath because the house had learned to hold them gently.

And then, underneath everything, my mother's voice. Young. Younger than I had ever known her.

*I don't know if I'm any good at this,* she said. *But I'm going to try so hard.*

I sat down on the floor of that hallway and cried the way you can only cry when you are eleven and have just learned that your parents were people first.

And when she died, he stayed, and when he died, the house kept working — kept listening, kept the whole street's small griefs and door-slams and apologies, because he had never thought to build in a way to make it stop.

It is very faint. It's getting fainter — I know that. The house is forgetting at last, the way everything does.
